column4: The section’s root gloss links the Lord’s name with remaining; here the descending messengers say they come only by His command and conclude that He is not forgetful, directly answering the fear of being left.
The section’s denial of divine severance meets God’s direct reassurance to Moses and Aaron, “إِنَّنِي مَعَكُمَا”: He is with them, hearing and seeing, when they fear Pharaoh.

The section cites the claim that the Lord is not forgetful; Moses answers Pharaoh that his Lord neither errs nor forgets (“وَلَا يَنسَىٰ”), repeating the image’s assurance in a different prophetic scene.

The section names the dictionary form ودّع as leaving or cutting a tie; here the command is “وَدَعْ أَذَاهُمْ,” to leave their harm, distinguishing withdrawal from an abuser’s conduct from abandoning the person addressed.

The section’s dictionary form استودعته means leaving something with another for safekeeping; “مُسْتَوْدَعَهَا” is paired with every creature’s settled place, and God knows both, making entrusted keeping part of divine provision.
The section’s dictionary form استودعته means a deposit entrusted for protection; this verse names “مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمُسْتَوْدَعٌ” in human creation, placing settlement and safekeeping together.
The section glosses فآوى as joining someone and giving refuge; these youths leave their people and are told “فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ,” trusting their Lord to spread mercy over them.

The section’s sheltering of the orphan reverses vulnerability; this verse recalls the believers’ fear of being seized, then says God sheltered them (“فَآوَاكُمْ”), strengthened them, and provided good things.
The section’s dictionary form آوى includes joining and sheltering; here the emigrants “أَوَوْا وَنَصَرُوا” those who came to them, making refuge a human practice of support.
The section brings together departure, taking refuge, and enrichment; this verse promises that one who emigrates for God will find many places of refuge and ample provision on earth.
The section’s claim that the Lord did not leave the Prophet meets the cave scene: when his companion grieves, he says God is with them (“إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا”), and God sends tranquility.

The section’s denied abandonment meets the three whose isolation made the earth seem constricted and who found no refuge except to God (“لَا مَلْجَأَ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِلَّا إِلَيْهِ”); the verse then says He turned toward them.

The section explains the orphan as one liable to be neglected; here two orphans’ treasure is guarded until they mature, by their Lord’s mercy, so their father’s goodness can continue protecting them after his death.
The section distinguishes being left behind from being cared for; this verse describes poor emigrants expelled from homes and property, who seek God’s bounty and support His cause.
The section’s image of need met with shelter is enacted by the hosts who welcome emigrants and prefer them over themselves (“وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ”), even when they themselves are in need.
The section’s root gloss for فأغنى includes being made rich; this verse says God is the one who “أَغْنَىٰ,” directly naming the provision that answers need.
The section names عائلًا for need and فأغنى for its answer; this verse pairs fear of “عَيْلَةً” (poverty) with God enriching people from His bounty (“يُغْنِكُمُ اللَّهُ”).
The section’s need-to-provision image is sharpened by this contrast: Satan threatens poverty, while God promises forgiveness and bounty, so fear of need does not define what follows.
The section’s عائلًا فأغنى presents need answered by provision; this verse says that if those marrying are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty (“يُغْنِهِمُ اللَّهُ”).

The section says the orphan’s name is linked in its dictionary explanation to neglected kindness, and contrasts shelter with driving away; this denier actively shoves the orphan away (“يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ”).
The section reads sheltering the orphan as the opposite of neglect; this rebuke says people fail even to honor the orphan (“لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ”).
The section’s orphan is someone whose care can be neglected; this command forbids consuming the orphans’ property or exchanging their good for bad, giving neglect a concrete material form.
The section connects the orphan with being taken in; this verse describes guardians testing orphans until maturity and then handing their property over, so care reaches the point of independence.
The section’s shelter and provision for the orphan are reversed by this warning: those who consume orphan property unjustly are consuming fire, a stark boundary against exploitation.
The section glosses the orphan’s name through neglect of his good; this verse says reforming orphans’ affairs is best (“إِصْلَاحٌ لَّهُمْ خَيْرٌ”), making attentive care the stated response.
The section’s youths find refuge after leaving their people in 18:16; this scene says God strengthened their hearts as they stood against their people, supplying the resolve that precedes refuge.
The section names the cave youths’ refuge in 18:16; here they ask their Lord for mercy and right guidance as they withdraw to the cave, giving the refuge its own prayerful beginning.
The section joins being left with being taken in; after Joseph is cast into a well in 12:15, a passing caravan finds him and treats him as a valuable discovery, reversing his brothers’ abandonment.

The section’s فآوى means bringing someone close and sheltering him; after Joseph is sold away from his family, the Egyptian who buys him tells his wife to give him an honorable lodging and considers adopting him.

The section’s orphan image is of a vulnerable child received into care; Pharaoh’s wife asks that the infant Moses be spared and kept, opening the household refuge that follows his separation from his mother.
The section joins separation with continued care; God tells Moses’ mother to place him in the river but promises, “إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ إِلَيْكِ,” that He will return him to her.
The section places shelter after separation; this later part of Moses’ story returns him to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she may not grieve, completing the rescue begun in 28:9.
The section’s image joins separation with continued care; Moses is placed in a chest and cast into the river, yet God says He cast love over him and raised him under His eye.

The section distinguishes departure from being actively driven away; Joseph’s brother proposes casting him into the well so a traveler will pick him up, a plan to remove him that leaves his safety precarious.
The section says a person can be left behind yet not abandoned by God; after Joseph’s brothers cast him into the well, God reveals that he will later remind them of what they did.

The section’s dictionary form قلا describes driving away; Abraham’s father threatens him and says “leave me for a long while,” a concrete human rejection set against the Lord’s refusal to abandon His servant.

The section distinguishes departure from divine abandonment; Abraham says he will leave his father and his people’s worship, showing a chosen separation from people and false gods rather than a rejected servant.
The section places care after separation; this neighboring verse says that after Abraham leaves his people, God grants him Isaac and Jacob, so departure is followed by new family and prophetic care.
The section rejects the idea that God has driven the Prophet away; this verse recalls people plotting to restrain, kill, or expel him, while God counters their plan.

The section’s second departure image is active expulsion; Shuaib’s people threaten to drive him and the believers from their town unless they return to their religion, a human rejection contrasted with divine care.
The section distinguishes a servant’s rejection from the Lord’s care; here disbelievers tell their messengers they will expel them unless they return, while God promises to destroy the wrongdoers.

The section’s dictionary gloss says the root ر ب ب can describe a cloud that lasts; this verse pictures the Lord extending shade and says He could have made it stationary, placing continuance under divine control.
The section pairs staying with departure; this neighboring verse says God withdraws the extended shade little by little, making a measured withdrawal the counterpart to the stationary shade of 25:45.
The section’s dictionary form for ر ب ب includes a cloud that persists; here God shades the Israelites with cloud and sends food, so the enduring sky-cover is part of care in their wilderness.

The section names a cloud that continues as a secondary dictionary sense; this verse again describes cloud shade over the Israelites alongside manna and quail, showing sustained provision in the wilderness.
The section glosses سجا with the dictionary form سكن (become still); this verse speaks of what “سَكَنَ فِي اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ,” linking the same settling sense to night and day under God’s care.
The section glosses سجا with the dictionary forms سكن ودام (became still and lasted); this verse calls night “سَكَنًا,” a direct formulation of the quiet night before the reassurance.
The section’s gloss for the night is stillness and duration; this verse says night was made so people may rest in it, giving that stillness a stated human purpose.
The section presents the night as settled before the denial of separation; this verse calls night a covering and sleep a rest, joining darkness to repose.
The section’s dictionary gloss for سجا includes quiet and duration; this verse says God made night for rest and day for seeking bounty, framing rest as part of mercy.
The section foregrounds the night’s stillness; this verse says God made night so people may rest in it, then calls daylight a means of seeing.
The section glosses سجا as becoming still (“سكن”); this verse calls sleep “سُبَاتًا,” a cessation and rest that gives another Quranic formulation of stillness.
The section’s night settles before the statement that God has not departed; this verse calls night a covering (“لِبَاسًا”), giving the dark its enveloping quality.
The section emphasizes night as still and lasting; this oath depicts night as it covers, a related night image that emphasizes concealment rather than settling.
The section’s night is glossed as settled and lasting; this oath depicts night as it covers the day, a distinct but related movement into darkness.
The section glosses سجا as a night that remains; this oath instead marks night as it withdraws, a direct reversal that makes the distinction between settling and departing visible.
The section’s dictionary gloss gives the night duration and stillness; this oath marks night as it passes on, the opposite temporal movement.
The section sets the still night before the reassurance; this neighboring verse makes the day a time of livelihood, completing the night-rest/day-activity contrast following 78:10.

The section’s dictionary form توديع الثوب means putting a garment in a case that preserves it; this verse uses clothing as a mutual covering between spouses, making protection a human relation as well as safekeeping.

The section’s dictionary form استودعته means entrusting a deposit for safekeeping; this verse says that when one person trusts another with a deposit, the trustee must return it, giving the keeping sense a human duty.
The section’s dictionary form وديعة is something left with another to preserve; this command to return trusts to their owners states the corresponding obligation of faithful keeping.
The section separates a farewell from a lasting abandonment; in a divorce context, this verse says not to forget generosity between people even when they part, showing care can survive separation.

The section examines what it means to leave someone; this verse forbids a husband from leaving a wife “as if suspended” (“كَالْمُعَلَّقَةِ”), naming the vulnerable in-between state that non-abandonment rules out.
The section says the Lord did not leave the Prophet; here the Prophet laments that his people have abandoned the Quran (“مَهْجُورًا”), reversing who has severed the relation.

The section’s image distinguishes rejection from care; here the Prophet is told to bear their words and avoid them graciously, a boundary showing that withdrawal from harm need not mean being forsaken.

The section’s dictionary form قلا العير آتنه describes a wild ass driving its mares away; this verse compares people fleeing to “حُمُرٌ مُّسْتَنفِرَةٌ,” reversing the agency, and 74:51 names the lion they flee from.
The section’s wild-ass dictionary scene has the male driving the mares; this neighboring verse identifies the wild asses’ pursuer as a lion, completing the reversal in 74:50.
The section’s denial of abandonment addresses prophetic distress; here God says He knows the Prophet’s breast is constricted by what people say, naming the hurt behind such reassurance.
The section’s reassurance is followed by worship rather than isolation; this neighboring verse tells the Prophet to glorify his Lord and prostrate in response to the distress named in 15:97.
The section puts continuing divine care beside the Prophet’s distress; this neighboring verse commands worship of the Lord until certainty comes, extending the response in 15:98.
The section notes that ر ب ب can name staying; this verse uses the related root in “رَبَّيَانِي” for parents raising a child, connecting the word family to sustained care for the young.

The section links the Lord’s name with staying and develops the taking-in of a vulnerable child; Pharaoh says “أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا” (“did we not raise you among us”), showing the same root family used for raising rather than staying.
The section glosses فآوى as joining someone; this verse says God joined the believers’ hearts, making their closeness itself a kind of refuge that human wealth could not create.
The section’s عائلًا فأغنى depicts need met by provision; after Moses helps two women and rests in shade, he asks his Lord for whatever good He sends, naming his own dependence.
The section says the needy person was met with enrichment; this verse assigns the asker and deprived a right in the wealthy people’s property, turning provision into an obligation.
The section’s need-to-enrichment image meets this statement that some wealth has a known right; 70:25 specifies the recipients as the asker and deprived.
The section’s provision for the needy is made concrete here: the known right in 70:24 belongs to the asker and the deprived.
The section gives need a place in the image of divine provision; this verse describes poor people who cannot travel to earn and do not beg insistently, making their need easy to overlook.
The section’s فأغنى answers need; this rebuke condemns failure to encourage feeding the poor, giving that provision a neglected social counterpart.
The section links the orphan’s neglect to need left uncared for; this neighboring verse condemns failure to urge feeding the poor, completing the actions of the denier in 107:2.
The section’s image ends in provision for need; this verse describes the condemned person as one who did not encourage feeding the poor, a specific opposite of enrichment.
The section glosses the orphan’s name through neglected care; this covenant expressly commands kindness to orphans, placing them among those owed good treatment.
The section’s orphan is a vulnerable person taken in; this description of righteousness includes giving wealth to orphans, a concrete form of care.
The section’s image pairs need with provision; this answer about spending names orphans among those for whom good wealth is spent.
The section’s orphan is one whose care can be neglected; this inheritance rule directs witnesses to give orphans and the poor something from the distribution and speak kindly to them.
The section connects sheltering an orphan to not neglecting his kindness; this command places orphans among neighbors to whom good treatment is owed.
The section’s provision answers vulnerability; this verse depicts the righteous feeding an orphan, the poor, and a captive despite their own love of the food.
The section’s orphan is a vulnerable person who needs care; this verse identifies feeding an orphan who is a relative as one of the hard paths of goodness.
The section connects the orphan with protection rather than neglect; this command forbids approaching orphan property except in the best manner, stating a boundary on the guardian’s conduct.
The section’s sheltering of an orphan reverses neglect; this command forbids approaching an orphan’s property except in the best way until maturity.
The section quotes the claim that the Lord is not forgetful; this verse says hypocrites forgot God and so were forgotten, a stated boundary that reverses the section’s assurance.
The section quotes the claim that the Lord is not forgetful; this verse says people forgot the meeting of this day and so are forgotten, making human neglect the boundary to the reassurance.
The section cites “your Lord is not forgetful”; here the wrongdoer first neglected God’s signs and is told, “today you are forgotten,” making human neglect the explicit reversal.
The section’s reassurance that God does not forget is bounded by this judgment: those who forgot the meeting of this day are told to taste the consequence of having forgotten it.
The section says the Lord is not forgetful; this judgment says, “today We forget you as you forgot the meeting of this day,” a direct reversal grounded in their own neglect.
The section’s denial of abandonment meets the consequence stated here: they are left in the Fire because they took God’s signs in mockery and worldly life deceived them, completing 45:34’s judgment.
